question: How many people were killed on October 7, 2023?

sideA.label: Israeli Government
sideA.text: 1,195 Israelis killed (revised from initial ~1,400). Includes ~859 civilians and ~336 military/security personnel. This is the most comprehensive verified count, cross-referenced by Israel Police, IDF, and forensic teams.

sideB.label: Hamas / Al Jazeera
sideB.text: Hamas does not dispute the scale of Israeli deaths but asserts the attack was a legitimate resistance operation against an occupying power. Some analysts note the initial Israeli figure of ~1,400 was inflated by counting foreign nationals who died and were later reclassified.

resolution: The revised Israeli figure of ~1,195 is accepted by major international bodies including the UN. The initial 1,400 figure has been revised down; 1,195 is now the official and most-cited count.

question: Did Hamas systematically use sexual violence as a weapon on October 7?

sideA.label: Israel / UN Special Representative
sideA.text: Yes. Israel presented extensive evidence including forensic reports, survivor testimony, and body camera footage to UN Special Representative Pramila Patten, who concluded there are 'reasonable grounds' to believe sexual violence occurred, including gang rape, sexual torture, and mutilation. The UN Security Council was briefed in March 2024.

sideB.label: Hamas / Palestinian Advocates
sideB.text: Hamas officially denies that sexual violence was ordered or systematic. Some journalists and advocates (notably in The Intercept and Al Jazeera) raised questions about specific cases and evidence methodology, arguing some early reports were based on unverified social media claims. Hamas called the allegations 'fabricated propaganda.'

resolution: The UN's own investigator (Pramila Patten) concluded there are 'reasonable grounds' to believe sexual violence occurred in a widespread and systematic manner on Oct 7. The IDF and Israeli Knesset committee have produced extensive documentation. On May 12, 2026 (Day 948), the Civil Commission on October 7th Crimes by Hamas — an independent two-year investigation led by Dr. Cochav Elkayam-Levy — published its final report concluding that sexual violence was 'systematic, widespread, and integral' to the October 7 attack: a deliberate, calculated military strategy, not spontaneous acts. New findings in the report include previously undisclosed evidence of sexual abuse of minors. Every case was cross-referenced with independent witness accounts and forensic evidence. The report is expected to be submitted to the ICC as evidentiary support for potential charges against Hamas commanders for sexual violence as a crime against humanity. Hamas continues to officially deny systematic sexual violence was ordered.

question: Who bears responsibility for the October 7 intelligence failure?

sideA.label: Opposition / Military Analysts
sideA.text: The intelligence failure was comprehensive: AMAN (military intelligence) had the Jericho Wall document for a year and dismissed it; female soldiers' warnings were ignored; IDF Southern Command was under-resourced partly due to West Bank settler protection duties; and the judicial reform crisis (with reservists refusing training) degraded readiness. Netanyahu's government bears political responsibility.

sideB.label: Netanyahu Government
sideB.text: Netanyahu has blamed the military and intelligence establishment, specifically Shin Bet Director Ronen Bar and IDF Chief Halevi, for operational failures. He has argued that political leadership was not given adequate warning. Netanyahu opposed establishing an independent commission with subpoena power.

resolution: IDF Chief of Staff Halevi and Shin Bet Director Bar both resigned in 2025 accepting responsibility. Multiple internal IDF investigations confirmed systemic failures. On April 27, 2026, the IDF released its final probe into the Kibbutz Holit attack — concluding the community was left undefended for 6 hours 53 minutes against ~60 Hamas Nukhba terrorists; 13 civilians and 3 soldiers killed. The same day, Israel's High Court of Justice granted the government 2 more months until July 1, 2026 to decide the form of a broader October 7 investigation. On May 5, 2026, outgoing IAF Commander Maj. Gen. Tomer Bar became the highest-ranking departing military official to explicitly call for an independent external probe at his handover ceremony. On May 12, 2026 (Day 948), Netanyahu's CBS 60 Minutes interview — his partial acknowledgment that 'everybody bears some responsibility, from the prime minister down' was his first explicit self-inclusion in culpability; Knesset passed 93-0 military tribunal law for ~300 October 7 perpetrators with death penalty for genocide. On May 13 (Day 949), the Kallner inquiry bill was revealed to have dropped 'independent investigation' language and added a 'no judges' clause. On May 27 (Day 963), IDF killed Hamas Al-Qassam Brigades commander Mohammed Odeh — the fourth senior October 7 architect eliminated in 2026. On May 28, a Knesset panel restored the word 'massacre' to the October 7 Memorial Day bill after backlash over its removal. On May 29 (Day 965), Imad Aqel was identified as the last surviving senior Hamas figure from the October 7 planning circle. On May 30 (Day 966): The IDF formally shut down its Hostages and Missing Persons HQ — 846 days after October 7 — after all 251 hostages were accounted for. On May 31 (Day 967): Haredi coalition parties threatened to back the independent October 7 probe unless the coalition advanced the ultra-Orthodox daycare subsidy bill. The Knesset advanced the daycare bill; the Kallner bill still requires three more plenum readings. On June 3–4, 2026 (Days 970–971): Haredi extremists attacked the home of Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg — smashing windows, shattering his car, and placing a swastika-marked flag — 62 arrested. Police later confirmed the attack was organized in advance with buses deliberately transporting rioters to harm the judge. Supreme Court President Isaac Amit called it 'a pogrom.' Netanyahu condemned it while sustaining the coalition parties driving the protest movement. Former Supreme Court President Beinisch (June 5) warned Israel was 'sliding toward anarchy.' On June 6, 2026 (Day 973): ~1,000 protesters rallied at Habima Square in Tel Aviv — the sister of a slain Gaza hostage accused the government of trying to 'erase the massacre, the abandonment, and its responsibility.' Netanyahu's appointment of his personal defense lawyer Michael Rabello as state comptroller became a focal protest grievance, as the comptroller is legally mandated to audit government conduct before and after October 7. On June 14, 2026, prosecutors indicted four Beit Shemesh men over the Sohlberg riot on rioting (and, for two of them, trespassing) charges. On June 24, 2026, Netanyahu concluded his own corruption-trial testimony after 98 hearings — a separate but politically entangled proceeding critics say he has used to bolster his case for judicial overhaul while resisting an independent October 7 commission. Israel's July 1, 2026 Supreme Court deadline passed with the government relying on the Knesset's in-progress Kallner bill rather than a fresh independent framework. Separately, on July 2, 2026, the High Court voided the Knesset's vote appointing Rabello as state comptroller after finding Likud lawmakers had photographed their supposedly secret ballots, ordering a revote; coalition figures floated delaying or defying it. The accountability pressure culminated in nationwide protests on July 2, 2026 marking 1,000 days since October 7, with demonstrators blocking Tel Aviv's Ayalon Highway and clashing with police outside the Knesset. On July 6, 2026, the Knesset passed the Kallner bill's first reading 59-0 amid a total opposition boycott — a politically-appointed (not independent, no-judges) commission structure that legal advisers say is designed for political control. The coalition explicitly used the vote to preserve the bill under the Knesset's continuity rule for the next parliament, having conceded it will not become law before dissolution. On July 12, 2026, Israel's election was formally set for October 27, 2026, with the Knesset dissolving July 17 — the first full four-year term since 1988 — making the unresolved independent-inquiry question a central campaign issue. Days before dissolution, on July 5, 2026, Netanyahu's Cabinet voted unanimously to defy a High Court ruling for the first time in Israeli history (on the broadcast media regulator), while Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana simultaneously confirmed he would not hold the court-ordered revote of Michael Rabello's state comptroller election — leaving Israel with no sitting comptroller, and thus no official empowered to audit government conduct on October 7, since that Sunday. All of Israel's living former Supreme Court chief justices called court defiance 'the final nail in the coffin of democracy.' The Knesset formally dissolved July 17, 2026 in a final legislative blitz (extending IDF service to 32 months, stripping attorney-general powers, and other measures) that left the Kallner bill unfinished. On July 22, 2026, the government formally told the High Court it could not complete October 7 probe legislation before the election, citing 'scheduling constraints' and asking petitions be dismissed; the October Council of bereaved and hostage families called this 'an unprecedented display of contempt for the court, the rule of law, and the Israeli public.' On August 8, 2026, Ruby and Hagit Chen — parents of slain hostage Itay Chen — rallied at Habima Square urging voters to back only parties pledging a state commission of inquiry. As of August 9, 2026 (Day 1037): no independent or political state commission of inquiry has been established, nearly three years after the attack; the Kallner bill remains stalled after its first reading and the government has deferred completion until after the October 27 election. JPPI (63%, May 15) and Hebrew University (72%, April 26) polls show broad public demand for an independent commission. The Beyachad alliance (Bennett-Lapid) pledges a Day-1 state commission if it wins the October 27 election. On August 11, 2026, the Tel Aviv Municipality formally renamed the Tel Aviv Museum plaza 'Hostages Square,' cementing the informal name used throughout the hostage-return campaign as accountability activism continued into the election season. On August 13, 2026, Eyal Eshel — father of slain Nahal Oz lookout soldier Roni Eshel — told KAN News that witness testimony he privately collected indicates some terrorists at the Nahal Oz base spoke Farsi on October 7, reinforcing intelligence assessments of Iranian proxy involvement in attack preparations, though physical presence of Iranian personnel during the assault itself remains unconfirmed; Eshel has separately called for a full state commission of inquiry. On August 19, 2026 (Day 1047), Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara told the High Court of Justice she supports postponing any decision on establishing a state commission of inquiry until a new government is formed after the October 27 election, calling a state commission 'clearly the most appropriate legal tool' while noting the government still hasn't acted nearly three years on; the Movement for Quality Government (representing 35,000+ petitioners) and the October Council rejected the delay, with the latter accusing the government of hoping 'time would cause people to forget the greatest disaster in the country's history.' On August 20, 2026 (Day 1049), the IDF's Military Advocate-General's Corps published its first war crimes report since October 7, reviewing 150+ Gaza-war investigations: a criminal Military Police probe was ordered into the January 2024 killing of six-year-old Hind Rajab and two paramedics who tried to reach her, with Maj.-Gen. Offir finding the monitoring officers at minimum grossly negligent; a second criminal probe was opened into the March 2025 killing of 15 Palestine Red Crescent paramedics; and the April 2024 World Central Kitchen strike that killed seven aid workers was closed without criminal charges, attributed to a surveillance misidentification of armed WCK security contractors as Hamas fighters. Critics noted the report addresses IDF conduct during the Gaza war rather than the pre-October 7 intelligence failure itself, leaving the core accountability question — an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures that preceded the attack — still unresolved ahead of the October 27 election. On August 22, 2026 (Day 1051), roughly 250 people attended the weekly Habima Square protest, where Liad Baram — father of Nahal Oz soldier Neta Baram, killed October 7 — said the state has an 'unceasing and unforgivable debt' to investigate the failures, accusing the system in power of continuing 'to blind us.' On August 24, 2026 (Day 1053), the October Council published 'Strategic Warning: Default 2026,' warning that the IDF's pre-October 7 containment mentality ('conceptzia') has persisted rather than disappeared, citing testimony that Hamas continues to rebuild and test the Yellow Line ceasefire boundary (14 violations logged in one 24-hour window per a leaked IDF report) while field observers who raise alarms are pressured into silence — echoes of the pre-attack dynamic the report says has merely 'changed shape.' A senior security official cited in the report said Netanyahu 'received more than ten warnings' before October 7 and dismissed them as exaggeration. The report reinforces the October Council's argument that, absent an independent state commission, the same institutional failures remain unaddressed heading into the October 27 election.

question: Did the IDF use the Hannibal Directive on October 7, potentially killing Israeli hostages?

sideA.label: Haaretz / Israeli Media Investigation
sideA.text: Evidence suggests IDF units, including helicopter pilots, fired on vehicles and structures containing Israeli hostages on October 7, possibly under Hannibal Directive protocol (kill to prevent capture). At least one Merkava tank fired on a house in Be'eri where ~12 Israelis were held hostage, killing some. Helicopter gunship fire killed some hostages being transported to Gaza.

sideB.label: IDF Spokesperson
sideB.text: The IDF has denied officially activating the Hannibal Directive on October 7. The IDF maintains that forces responded to legitimate military threats. IDF statements acknowledge that some friendly fire occurred in the chaos of battle but reject the characterization of deliberate hostage-killing policy.

resolution: Ongoing IDF internal investigations and Knesset committee inquiries. Haaretz and NYT reporting based on official documents and testimonies is credible. IDF denials of a formal Hannibal order do not exclude individual unit decisions. Full accountability remains unresolved.

question: Should Israel have prioritized hostage deals over continued military operations in Gaza?

sideA.label: Hostage Families Forum / Opposition
sideA.text: Families consistently argued that Netanyahu delayed or sabotaged ceasefire deals (particularly in May 2024 and November 2024) in order to satisfy far-right coalition partners (Smotrich, Ben Gvir) who opposed any ceasefire. The Forum accused Netanyahu of 'abandoning' hostages for political survival. Benny Gantz resigned from the war cabinet in June 2024 over the lack of a post-war strategy.

sideB.label: Netanyahu Government / Right Wing
sideB.text: Netanyahu argued that military pressure — specifically the Rafah operation — was necessary to produce genuine Hamas concessions in hostage deals. He maintained that Hamas was using ceasefire negotiations as a tactic to survive rather than return hostages. Far-right coalition partners (Ben Gvir, Smotrich) threatened to collapse the government if a permanent ceasefire was agreed.

resolution: The January 2025 ceasefire deal occurred after significant military degradation of Hamas and the deaths of Sinwar and Haniyeh. Whether earlier deals were possible or blocked by Netanyahu remains a central political controversy in Israel. Hostage families held major weekly protests outside Netanyahu's residence throughout 2024.

question: Did Hamas time the attack to exploit Israel's internal judicial reform crisis?

sideA.label: Israeli Security Analysts
sideA.text: Yes. Hamas leaders, including Yahya Sinwar, specifically referenced Israel's unprecedented internal division over judicial reform in internal documents. Reserve officers' refusal to train during judicial reform protests degraded IDF readiness. AMAN internal reports noted that Hamas was monitoring Israeli public discord. The timing on Simchat Torah (Jewish holiday when many soldiers are with family) was also deliberate.

sideB.label: Hamas Official Narrative
sideB.text: Hamas stated the attack was in response to Israeli incursions at Al-Aqsa Mosque, settler violence in the West Bank, and the ongoing Gaza blockade. Hamas denied that internal Israeli politics drove the timing. Mohammed Deif's announcement cited Palestinian 'resistance' motivations rather than Israeli weakness.

resolution: Sinwar's own captured personal notes and communications, reviewed by the Meir Amit Intelligence Center, reference Israeli societal divisions. The attack timing on a Jewish holiday and during peak division aligns with exploitation of Israeli vulnerability, though Hamas publicly frames it as a response to Palestinian oppression.

question: How many Hamas and allied fighters infiltrated Israel on October 7?

sideA.label: IDF / Israeli Government
sideA.text: Approximately 3,000 Hamas and allied militant fighters (including Palestinian Islamic Jihad, PFLP, and ordinary Gaza civilians who followed through the breach) crossed into Israel. The IDF identified ~1,500 killed inside Israel on Oct 7, implying ~1,500 returned to Gaza.

sideB.label: Hamas / Independent Analysts
sideB.text: Hamas's own operational planning documents described a force of approximately 3,000 fighters for the operation. Some analysts estimate 2,500–4,000 crossed total, including organized militants and civilians who followed through opened gaps. The IDF figure of 3,000 is widely accepted.

resolution: There is broad consensus around ~3,000 fighters plus additional individuals who crossed through fence breaches. The IDF's figure is the most-cited and is consistent with Hamas planning documents. Exact numbers remain uncertain.

question: Who was responsible for the Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital explosion on October 17, 2023?

sideA.label: Hamas / Palestinian Authority / Arab States
sideA.text: An Israeli airstrike hit Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital, killing up to 500 people according to Gaza Ministry of Health's initial statement. Hamas called it a 'war crime' and proof of Israel's targeting of civilian infrastructure. Several Arab leaders canceled a planned summit with President Biden.

sideB.label: Israel / US / Western Governments
sideB.text: A failed rocket launch by Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) caused the explosion — the rocket malfunctioned and hit the hospital parking lot. US, Canadian, and French intelligence agencies independently analyzed intercepts and satellite data and concluded an Israeli airstrike was not responsible. Death toll was also revised significantly below 500.

resolution: US, Canadian, French, and UK intelligence all concluded the explosion was caused by a failed Palestinian rocket, not an Israeli strike. Satellite imagery shows no crater consistent with an Israeli bomb. The death toll was far below Gaza MoH's initial estimate of 500. Most Western governments accept the misfired-rocket explanation; Hamas and Palestinian Authority maintain the Israeli airstrike narrative.

question: Were babies and children beheaded by Hamas fighters on October 7?

sideA.label: Israeli Officials / Some Media Reports
sideA.text: Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Netanyahu and government spokespeople, stated that Hamas fighters beheaded babies and committed atrocities against children. Some early media reports cited soldier testimonies of decapitated infants. The claims circulated globally and were cited by President Biden ('confirmed' he saw photographs).

sideB.label: Investigative Journalists / Fact-Checkers
sideB.text: Several journalists (notably from HuffPost, The Intercept) found the original source of 'beheaded babies' claims to be a single Israeli soldier whose statement was unverified. The IDF and Israeli government ultimately stated they could not confirm specific decapitation cases of infants. Biden's White House later clarified he had not personally seen photographs of beheaded babies.

resolution: Hamas committed well-documented atrocities against children on October 7, including killings in homes and safe rooms. The specific claim of 'beheaded babies' as a systematic practice was not confirmed by IDF forensic reports or Israeli government officials, though mutilations of adult victims were documented. The claim became a significant information warfare flashpoint.

question: How effective was Iron Dome against the October 7 rocket barrage?

sideA.label: IDF / Israeli Defense Establishment
sideA.text: Iron Dome achieved an approximately 85–90% interception rate overall on October 7, consistent with its historic performance. The system successfully protected Tel Aviv and Jerusalem. The volume of simultaneous launches (~2,000+ in first 20 minutes) was designed to overwhelm batteries in the south, where interception rates were lower.

sideB.label: Military Critics / Analysts
sideB.text: Iron Dome fundamentally failed its core mission on October 7 in the Gaza Envelope. By concentrating so many rockets simultaneously, Hamas demonstrated a systematic saturation strategy that Iron Dome cannot defeat. The system's reliance on missile interceptors (each costing ~$50,000 vs. Hamas Qassam rockets at ~$800) is economically unsustainable at scale.

resolution: Iron Dome performed within its design parameters but was deliberately overwhelmed by Hamas's massed-launch strategy. The IDF has acknowledged this tactical vulnerability and invested in additional batteries and the David's Sling / Arrow systems for improved layered defense.

question: Is Israel's response to October 7 a genocide under international law?

sideA.label: South Africa / Many Global South Nations
sideA.text: South Africa's ICJ application argued that Israel's conduct in Gaza — including the scale of civilian deaths, destruction of homes, hospitals, and food supply infrastructure, siege conditions, and statements by Israeli officials — constitutes genocide under the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. Over 50 countries filed interventions supporting the case.

sideB.label: Israel / United States / Germany
sideB.text: Israel and its Western allies reject the genocide characterization. Israel argues it is conducting legitimate military operations against a terrorist organization that uses civilians as shields, provides humanitarian corridors, and has specific military objectives. Germany, Canada, and the US have all challenged the genocide framing in legal filings.

resolution: The ICJ issued provisional measures in January 2024 finding a 'plausible' risk of genocide and ordering Israel to take measures to prevent it, but stopped short of ordering a ceasefire. The full genocide case continues at the ICJ. Whether Israel's actions meet the legal threshold of genocidal intent ('dolus specialis') remains a contested legal question. International humanitarian law experts are divided.

question: Did Egypt warn Israel about a coming Hamas attack before October 7?

sideA.label: Egyptian Sources / Reports
sideA.text: Egyptian intelligence officials told AP and other outlets that Egypt warned Israel 'repeatedly' in the days before October 7 that something 'big and unusual' was coming from Hamas. An Egyptian intelligence official said they warned Israel through multiple channels that Hamas was planning 'something big' in the days before the attack.

sideB.label: Israeli Government
sideB.text: Israel's government disputed the claim that Egypt provided specific, actionable warnings about an imminent attack. Israeli officials said Egypt may have passed generic threat assessments but not intelligence specific enough to trigger a full military response. IDF and Shin Bet have not acknowledged receiving specific Egyptian warnings.

resolution: Egyptian officials' claims of repeated specific warnings were reported by AP and other outlets. The IDF and Israeli government have not confirmed receiving specific, actionable warnings from Egypt. This claim is contested and remains unresolved, with neither side releasing full documentation.

question: Did Hamas use hospitals and civilian infrastructure as military bases?

sideA.label: IDF / US Intelligence
sideA.text: Israel presented evidence — including maps, live footage from raids, and captured Hamas documents — that Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City served as Hamas's main command and intelligence center, with tunnels running beneath it. CIA Director Bill Burns confirmed US intelligence assessed Al-Shifa as having military use. IDF forces raided the hospital in November 2023 and presented weapons caches, surveillance equipment, and tunnel entrances.

sideB.label: Hamas / Doctors / WHO
sideB.text: Hamas denied using hospitals as military bases. Doctors at Al-Shifa said they saw no Hamas command center. The WHO and MSF noted the IDF presented limited direct evidence of active command and control inside the hospital itself. Critics argued the IDF's original claims were exaggerated compared to what was actually found in the November 2023 raid.

resolution: IDF evidence showed tunnel access points beneath Al-Shifa and weapons caches inside the compound. The scale of the 'command center' was disputed — evidence supported military use of tunnels beneath the hospital but did not confirm active command operations in the hospital itself during the raid. Hamas use of civilian infrastructure for tunnels and weapons storage is broadly documented by multiple sources.

question: Has October 7 made a two-state solution more or less likely?

sideA.label: International Community / Palestinian Authority
sideA.text: The international community (US, EU, Saudi Arabia) has increased pressure for a two-state solution as the only durable path to peace. Saudi Arabia indicated normalization with Israel would require a credible pathway to Palestinian statehood. Spain, Norway, and Ireland formally recognized Palestine in May 2024. International support for Palestinian statehood has grown significantly since October 7.

sideB.label: Israeli Right Wing / Netanyahu Government
sideB.text: For Netanyahu's coalition, October 7 reinforced opposition to Palestinian statehood — Finance Minister Smotrich and National Security Minister Ben Gvir explicitly stated Gaza should be re-settled by Israelis. Netanyahu has consistently opposed Palestinian statehood. Israeli public support for a two-state solution dropped dramatically following October 7. Some Israeli analysts argue October 7 has made coexistence impossible in the medium term.

resolution: October 7 simultaneously increased international pressure for a two-state solution while making it politically impossible in Israel's current right-wing government. The PA's legitimacy in Gaza has been effectively eliminated. A functional two-state solution pathway requires resolution of the Gaza governance question, hostage crisis, and rebuilding — none of which have concrete international plans as of 2026.

question: Is Phase Two of the Gaza ceasefire — Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawal — achievable in 2026?

sideA.label: US / International Community
sideA.text: The Board of Peace plan unveiled in March 2026 outlines an eight-month, multiphase process for Hamas to decommission offensive weapons while Israel progressively withdraws. The US, Qatar, and Egypt believe a workable pathway exists if both sides show good faith. 27 countries signed the Board of Peace framework. UN Gaza reconstruction funding ($50B+) can only be unlocked once governance and security guarantees are in place.

sideB.label: Hamas / Netanyahu Government
sideB.text: Hamas refuses to fully disarm without a guaranteed Israeli withdrawal and progress toward Palestinian statehood — conditions Israel's far-right coalition refuses to accept. Netanyahu insists on full Hamas demilitarization before any withdrawal, arguing Hamas would reconstitute. Chatham House analysts warned in early 2026 that Phase Two 'will fail without a political vision,' as neither side has agreed on post-war Gaza governance.

resolution: As of June 7, 2026 (Day 974 / Ceasefire Day 241), Phase Two remains in total deadlock. All four Board of Peace deadlines (Apr 11, 14, 19, late-Apr window) passed without Hamas acceptance. On May 20–21, the Board of Peace published its six-month progress report identifying Hamas as the 'principal obstacle' to Phase Two and presented it to the UN Security Council, calling Hamas demilitarization 'non-negotiable.' Hamas rejected the report. Foreign Policy (June 5) reported the Board of Peace effectively 'stalled out,' with the Iran war diverting diplomatic attention. The Gaza ceasefire death toll (from documented Israeli violations) passed 1,000 on June 17, 2026, and reached 1,084+ killed / 3,491+ wounded by early July per Gaza MoH; OHCHR's Volker Türk said the pattern reflects 'continuing disregard for Palestinian lives, enabled by sweeping impunity,' citing further fatal strikes on July 6 and July 8. On July 6, 2026, Hamas announced the resignation of its Gaza civil administration under the Board of Peace framework, while the Board reiterated that Hamas disarmament is 'non-negotiable' — still under $1B of $17B pledged reconstruction funds received against the UN-EU-WB's $71.4B assessed rebuilding cost. Imad Aqel (Hamas logistics/tunnel commander) remained the sole surviving senior figure from the October 7 planning circle as of August 9, 2026, with the Al-Qassam Brigades supreme command still publicly vacant more than 10 weeks after Odeh's death; Hamas sources told Asharq Al-Awsat the group is weighing a 'collective leadership' model for the Qassam Brigades rather than naming him supreme commander, to avoid making him a singular target. Phase Two remains unresolved. This deadlock, combined with Israel's unresolved October 7 accountability crisis — the Kallner inquiry bill passed only a first reading (59-0, July 6) before the Knesset's July 17 dissolution, and the government told the High Court on July 22 it would not complete the legislation before the election — now defines the run-up to Israel's October 27, 2026 election.

question: Has Israel deliberately caused famine conditions in Gaza?

sideA.label: UN / Humanitarian Organizations
sideA.text: UNRWA, WFP, WHO, and the IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification) confirmed famine conditions in northern Gaza by early 2024. Deliberate aid restrictions, fuel cutoffs, and destruction of food supply chains created catastrophic food insecurity for 2.3 million Gazans.

sideB.label: Israel / US (initially)
sideB.text: Israel maintained it facilitated humanitarian aid entry through Kerem Shalom and other crossings and denied deliberately causing famine. Israel blamed Hamas for diverting aid, UNRWA for operational failures, and Egypt for delays at the Rafah crossing. The US initially supported Israel's position but by early 2024 began conditioning arms transfers on aid access improvements.

resolution: The UN's IPC and multiple humanitarian agencies confirmed famine conditions in northern Gaza by mid-2024. The ICC prosecutor cited starvation as a weapon of war in the arrest warrant application against Netanyahu and Gallant. The US State Department's own assessment (2024) found Israel had impeded aid delivery. Israel partially increased access after US pressure.

question: Were UNRWA employees involved in the October 7 attack?

sideA.label: Israel
sideA.text: Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Netanyahu, say a portion of UNRWA's staff took part in the October 7 massacre and that the agency has fostered anti-Israel indoctrination and collaborated with Hamas in Gaza. On August 25, 2026, Netanyahu cited this as grounds for dismantling an UNRWA vocational training center in Kafr Aqab, East Jerusalem, under the 2024 Israeli law banning UNRWA from operating on Israeli territory. That same week, the US State Department and USAID's Office of Inspector General announced the debarment of Hafez Mousa Mohammed Mousa, a former UNRWA school principal who coordinated communications with Hamas members during the October 7 attack — the first US debarment of a terrorist affiliated with a UN humanitarian agency — and proposed debarring three more former UNRWA teachers over October 7/Hamas/Islamic Jihad ties. Washington Free Beacon reporting citing the USAID probe separately confirmed Faisal Ali Al-Naami, an UNRWA 'social worker' filmed dragging slain hostage Yonatan Samerano's body into an SUV at Kibbutz Be'eri on October 7, was an active Hamas operative (he was killed in October 2023 and so was not himself debarred). USAID OIG has now flagged more than 100 current or former UNRWA staff over October 7 participation or Hamas/Islamic Jihad affiliation.

sideB.label: UNRWA / UN
sideB.text: UNRWA denies the accusations. A UN internal investigation into 19 employees Israel flagged found 9 may have been involved in the October 7 attacks and terminated their employment, while it found insufficient or no evidence against the others. A separate independent review (the Colonna review) identified neutrality-safeguard weaknesses at UNRWA but said Israel had not substantiated its broader claim that the agency's workforce as a whole was compromised. UNRWA has not issued a specific public response to the August 2026 USAID OIG debarment findings.

resolution: The evidentiary record is mixed and contested: the UN's own probe substantiated involvement for roughly half of the specific employees Israel named, not the broader institutional collaboration Israel alleges. Israel has continued to use the October 7 allegations as the legal and political basis for barring and now physically dismantling UNRWA facilities, most recently the Kafr Aqab center on August 25, 2026; UNRWA maintains it has a legal right to the site under a 1952 Jordanian land grant. A separate, US-domestic evidentiary track produced its first concrete sanctions on August 26-27, 2026: USAID OIG's investigation led the State Department to debar one former UNRWA principal and propose debarring three more former UNRWA staff, while newly attributing active Hamas-operative status to Al-Naami, the UNRWA worker filmed moving a hostage's body on October 7. This adds an independently-sourced (non-Israeli-government) evidentiary strand to Israel's broader claim, though the scope remains narrower than the full-workforce collaboration allegation UNRWA and the Colonna review dispute.
